utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Registrar, have the accused brought in, please. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does everybody hear? Are the interpreters ready? Good morning everybody, the Prosecution, Defence, General Blaskic, do you hear me? Two bits of information that I would like to give you. We will not sit on Monday for reasons which you already know, nor on Wednesday. I am telling you this so that the Defence counsel can take all -- make all the arrangements that they need and that there be no surprises. There are difficulties which have arisen from the new judges who are coming and ceremonies that are accompanying the inauguration of the new judges. Mr. Cayley -- I believe it was Mr. Nobilo, I am sorry. Mr. Nobilo, you had begun your cross-examination. Good morning, Mr. Ahmic, did you rest well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, yes, I am feeling fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine, then we can begin. ABDULAH AHMIC (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. Ahmic. Let us continue where we left off last night. Tell me, is it true to say that there was a mobilisation and that everyone up to the age of 60 was mobilised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you referring to Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am asking you about the Muslims now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You must tell me the period, what dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: My question is before the conflicts, the conflicts in 1993 in April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Will you tell me, please, whether I am right in saying that your brother, the late Muris, was against the conflict with the Croats at the barricades and that as a result, he was detained at the school in Ahmici and then during the night transferred to the house of Mehmed Ahmic and placed under house arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is completely untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You told the Prosecutor during the examination-in-chief that you were not allowed to carry weapons, so my question is: did this apply to the main road and the town of Vitez and were you allowed to wear weapons within Ahmici itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Weapons could be carried in upper Ahmici, where the HVO forces had not entered during the first conflict, whereas in the lower part of the village of Ahmici, near the road and in Zume, weapons could not be carried.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did your patrols nevertheless patrol the lower part of Ahmici after all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were there weapons in the lower part of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was probably brought there, but if it was carried, it was concealed, because people were not allowed to carry weapons openly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, prior to the outbreak of the conflict in April 1993, did you have any checkpoint on the road through Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not quite understand your question. Could you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes. In April 1993, or rather just prior to April 1993, did you set up a checkpoint within the village of Ahmici on the small road running through the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, the checkpoint existed up to 20th October 1992. There were no checkpoints in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who held that checkpoint? Was it held by the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was held by the TO. That was the entrance to the village of Ahmici near the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In October 1992, you told us that you were in the school next to the radio transmitter in the night prior to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the same room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not in the same room. I was near the school at the time, nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did a message come from someone to remove that checkpoint, or a threat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that a messenger came from the settlement of Zume, sent by the Croats, to contact our people who were there near the school and he told them that Dario Kordic had sent a message saying that if we did not remove the barricade immediately, we would be attacked in the morning and set fire to, and this in effect happened in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, please, is it true that the BH-Army in Vitez municipality was founded somewhere in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it true that Midhat Brbic became the commander of the BH-Army in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it true that this meant an improved organisation than existed up until then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It should have been that way, but it was not possible to make any improvements because of a shortage of equipment. It was an organisation on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But how do you compare this to the previous period, to the month of October with the establishment of the BH-Army at the beginning of 1993, was the situation improved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that in Ahmici, the situation was worse. As for Vitez, I cannot tell you because I was not familiar with the situation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let me read to you now an excerpt from your statement which you gave to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal. It is a statement signed on 3rd February 1995, for the Prosecution it is on page 5. I shall try and read it in English, so will you have it translated: "In December, the Territorial Defence in the Vitez area was called 'Bosnian Army'. The organisation was a little bit better. The headquarters of the army was in Vitez. The commander of the BH-Army in Ahmici was Midhat Brbic and the commander in Vitez was Sefkija Djidic. There were no barracks in Ahmici. In 1993 there was still a village guard in the village of Ahmici. It functioned in the same way as in 1992." Was that what you told the investigators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, only I must say that the organisation in Ahmici was not so good.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Will you tell me now, you had these village guards and you had the BH-Army. Was there a criterion according to which some men belonged to the BH and others to the village guards? How was this divided in Ahmici among the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, there were criteria. The younger men joined the BH-Army formations on paper, and the older men kept guard duty. They were mostly older people, they continued to perform the function of Civil Defence, if you could call it that, or Territorial Defence, if you prefer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that this was on paper. Tell me, these young men who joined the BH-Army, did they live separately in a barracks or did they continue living in their homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Ahmici, most of them lived in their own homes. Occasionally, they went to barracks. In Kruscica there was a barracks and in Preocica, but very rarely did they go there. They probably had some kind of training.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So they did not live in Kruscica but they went there for training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the brigade that you came under was called the 325th Mountain Brigade and it was based in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly where it was based, but I know that within the command structure, there was a sort of vacancy, the commander was Dzananovic and Kelesutra should have come and I know that for a long time, it was not clear who was in command. I do not know whether you are familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it true that young men -- that the company command was in Vrhovine, it was the command for the company to which the young men from Ahmici belonged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it true that the battalion command that young men from Ahmici came under was in Preocica and they went there for parade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a part belonged to the Preocica and another part to Kruscica. It depended on the assignments they were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So the commander of the BH-Army was Midhat Brbic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, who was his deputy, his assistant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Senad Sisic was his deputy, then Hidzro, we called him, Bilic. Hidzro is a nickname, I am not sure of his first name, Hajrudin? In the village of Pirici he had somebody we called Dzegir. He had an assistant, Nermin Kermo. Those were his assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And the young men from Ahmici were joined by whom, the young men from Zume, Santici, Pirici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And Nadioci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know about Nadioci. They were not with us in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So we have the BH-Army and the 325th Brigade. What about the village guards, how were they structured? Who was in command there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muris, in the same way that Muris acted, so Midhat Brbic acted similarly, only in my view not as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So Midhat Brbic was the commander of both the army and of the village guards in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was all one and the same. The only difference being that the guards were reinforced by elderly retired people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, before the conflict in April 1993, were these guard duties organised regularly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In March and April, before the outbreak of the conflict in 1993, were these guard duties taken seriously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not really, the discipline was not very high, because there was no military police to discipline these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us go on to the conflicts prior to the actual conflict in April. To refresh your memory, do you remember any problems occurring in Travnik, around Easter, the hoisting of Croatian flags; did you hear rumours of that in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, sir, I am not informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were you informed that in Zenica the commander of the HVO brigade, Totic, had been kidnapped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know Sesko from Grabovi, who was among other things elected representative of Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sezahir Pezer, but they call him Sesko, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know that on 7th March 1993, when Sesko was on duty, there were attempts to disarm the guards in Ahmici, that there was some exchange of fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whose guards?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The Ahmici guards.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But who tried to disarm them?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO? No, I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know that on 11th March, Ramiz from upper Ahmici was disarmed when on guard duty.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who was he disarmed by?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: By people from Gornji Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Ramiz from Grabovi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of that either. I was not living in upper Ahmici, I was living on the other side of the road, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am just asking. Five days before the outbreak of the conflict, it was a Sunday and the conflict occurred on Friday in April 1993, therefore on 11th April 1993, were you aware that there was a meeting in the school at 5.00 pm, the command was holding a meeting and the frontlines were agreed upon should fighting break out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that there was a meeting, but I do not know whether it was then. I know that the Croats also had a meeting on Sunday at the cemetery, where they probably agreed on the way they would attack. It was a very large meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Are you referring to the cemetery on the main road next to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because when they were coming away from that meeting, there was also some shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And who were the people attending that meeting, the Croats from which places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was an enormous rally, all the people from the environs had come. There were many cars, I do not know who they all were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was that on Sunday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you have a meeting on that Sunday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know there was a meeting, but I am not sure whether it was on Sunday. As for the establishment of the lines, I think that that was not discussed, but rather an analysis was made of the life of the population in Zume, who were in a difficult position, and the question was whether they should stay and live there or should they be moved elsewhere. I know that that was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you attend that meeting or did someone tell you about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know about this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, well that one, were you present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was present at the meeting at which we discussed the question of Zume.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know that on Sunday, April 11th, the Sunday prior to the conflict, a telegram came, placing troops on top alert in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but very soon after that, another message arrived lifting the order on combat readiness, so that for a time, this first degree of alert was not in effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who sent this telegram?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It probably came from the headquarters up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is my information true, that this telegram placing units in top alert arrived on Sunday 11th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact date, but I am aware that there was such a telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In any event, we are talking about a date prior to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you recall 13th April, so the following Tuesday, that Croats beat up Budu from Vrhovine so that all the young men from Ahmici went over there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know on 14th April, two days before the conflict, a three-barrelled weapon came to Zume and Emir was taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was Emir Pezer, he was going to work in Novi Travnik, and I know that he was taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could that have been on 14th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did a sniper shoot twice from Finka's house on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On 15th April 1993, that is one day before the conflict, did you receive information that Croats were grouping around the Kupreskic houses, and that there was a meeting of the command at 8.00 in the evening, that took place in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that there was a meeting between Croats and the representatives of Muslims in Vitez, and then they said, "everything is going to be sorted out and there will be no conflict", so that is what I know of. I do not know about a meeting around Kupreskic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You did not quite understand my question. The Croats started assembling, started grouping around the Kupreskic houses, and because of that the Muslims held a meeting at another place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know that on 15th April in the evening ammunition was distributed to the Muslims in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I would have gotten it had it been distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were you in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Which company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Company? I was part of the headquarters in Preocica but I never went over there, because it was not very active up there. I know that I was part of the battalion in Preocica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were you issued a rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not have a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you could not have received any ammunition on that evening either?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. Had there been any organisation of defence, I would have received both a rifle and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yesterday, you told us that some time in October there were about 100 to 120 members of the TO according to your estimate, and what I am interested in, this is in Ahmici, were there any refugees there --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am going to object to this point. There has been during the cross-examination substantial re-cross-examination about matters that were covered yesterday and this particular matter, I have a note that I took which expressly states Mr. Ahmic has already given an estimate of the numbers of TO who were in the village. If you wish, Mr. Nobilo can cover everything he did again yesterday, but then the re-examination will be much lengthier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, my learned colleague obviously did not understand me. I just introduced my question, and now my direct question was going to be: did any refugees arrive after October, and any fresh soldiers? That is the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The point I am making, Mr. President, is there has been substantial coverage of matters that were cross-examined yesterday. I have not made an objection to this point, in order to allow matters to proceed, but I do believe that Mr. Nobilo should be requested to cover areas that he did not cover yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Unless the judges have a computer memory, I do not remember all the details about certain questions. Personally, it seems to me that there are many questions that are asked, I am not sure -- I am speaking for both the Prosecution and the Defence, and you know my point of view, I am not really sure that everything is important for the discussion in order to arrive at whether General Blaskic is guilty or not. This is the danger, in fact, of these types of long questioning on this or that point. If one looks at the transcript, there might be repetition. I am trying to be attentive. I do not really remember though. I will ask my colleagues to help me on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I wanted to speak with my colleagues, because through the objection raised by Mr. Cayley, we have reached the very heart of this procedure which you know very well. My colleagues and myself consider that we agree on these following points. One, this is a point we have already stated, that the cross-examination must relate to the questions of the examination-in-chief. We cannot waiver on that point, but the second point which is raised today is that the cross-examination, and this is for the Prosecutor as well, questions must not be asked a second time, even in another form, by the Defence attorney in relation to his own cross-examination. I explained this, but I wanted to say it to Mr. Nobilo today, on another day, I may say it to Mr. Kehoe and Mr. Harmon. In truth, one must not go back to questions already asked, even by changing them somewhat. That is the first point. The second point, which is very important for the judges speaking to you, is that you must get the essential point of this trial to be focused on the guilt or non-guilt of General Blaskic. There is a fundamental point here and I first turn to the Prosecutor who has the initiative of being the Prosecutor. It is true, Mr. Cayley, that when you call in 300 witnesses you can well imagine we will run into problems, because the witness who comes today -- Ahmici today, another day there will be ten witnesses talking about a different village, this or that village. The right of the Defence will, of course, be able to challenge it. This is a real effort required here. I say this to you and I am saying it to the other sides as well. We judges, I say this to you in a very solemn fashion, we do not have computer memories, but we pay great attention. All of us take notes and we are very attentive. On this particular point, my own memory was somewhat faulty, but my colleagues are also very attentive. Therefore I will summarise. The two points are during the examination and the cross-examination which already takes a great deal of time, must not be used so that either the Prosecution or Defence lawyer once again asks the same questions even if it is asked differently. We will be attentive to that. The second point, and here we are becoming more and more stern about what we are saying, we will not hesitate to interrupt. We have been working together since 25th June, you have seen we have given warnings, different types of notification. What is of interest to the Tribunal is the guilt of General Blaskic as someone responsible for command responsibility, otherwise we will still be here in ten years. Obviously we do not always want to interrupt you, because the rights of the Defence are sacred and the Prosecution must be carried out as effectively and efficiently as possible. I do not have the entire case file in front of me, but we do have a feeling for when we are moving away from the essential. There come times, Mr. Nobilo, that I say to myself, "I want to interrupt him. Does this have something to do with General Blaskic's responsibility?" You can answer, "yes, it does", and I understand. The questions which you are seeking to find out is how was the army organised, what was the presence of the BH-Army, that is important, but please ask one or two questions to know whether in this or that form, on this or that date, there was a Bosnian defence. These are the questions that we are going -- in which we are going to get lost and we will not find our way back, not us, not you, not the Prosecution. The Tribunal will become increasingly firm. I say this to you, we will speak about it during a Status Conference, I promise you this, we should think about the length of this trial, and we will not hesitate to state what can be said and what cannot be said. We will limit the number of witnesses, if necessary. This Tribunal cannot permit itself to spend five years trying the responsibility of General Blaskic. I say this to you very clearly. Of course, everything is nuanced and you must have faith in the judges. When we interrupt you, we are being very careful, but please, these are the two fundamental points, I am speaking for my colleagues, please do not repeat questions even if they are asked in a different way in order to destabilise the witness, because we will protect the witness under those circumstances, I tell you that, to get right to the essential, the Defence and the Prosecution, and this should go through the limiting of the number of witnesses and then the cross-examination should then follow the initiative which belongs to the Prosecutor. These are the two points I wanted to say to you, even if I say it with passion and some vehemence, but I say it firmly and these are points that we will talk about again during the Status Conference. Mr. Nobilo, try to shorten the questions now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your permission, I would like to clarify two things. What is absolutely essential for the Defence is to ascertain the presence or absence of the BH-Army in Ahmici. This is absolutely essential for the Defence, and this is the essence of the Defence and the Defence cannot renounce that. This witness has said in the cross-examination that there was no BH-Army in Ahmici, and concerning the details, I accept that the details per se may not be very significant, but I have a document here which speaks of the defence of Ahmici, of the positions of people. This is a log book of a commander, so through talking about the details, I confirm that this plan of defence of Ahmici did exist, and I will try to speed things up, because we are very interested in speeding it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is a fact of different legal cultures. I am not challenging, and I think I am speaking for my colleagues, I am not challenging that point, but do recognise as regards the method, and I turn to the Prosecution as well, there are many things that can be said. I am saying this to you, that the rules give us a great deal of power. We have not used that power but will not hesitate to do so. Let me give you an example which comes from your own example. You have just said exactly what the essential thing is. Could you not have said it yesterday already? You could have said, "all right, Mr. Ahmic, what interests us in defending General Blaskic is", the point which you have just mentioned, "we have a document, we are going to submit it to you, and you will tell us what you think about it", then we will ask you questions. Then, of course, the Prosecutor can respond and also ask questions. That is what would be simpler, whereas here, we are kind of playing a game of cat and mouse, as we say in French, through little questions that are asked in order to destabilise. You are dealing with professional judges, you do not have a jury. Artificial destabilisation of witnesses is not something that we are interested in. I believe you might simply have said, "Mr. Ahmic, what the Defence is looking for is to learn how and where the Bosnian army were at the time of the events. That is what is interesting to us in relation to General Blaskic's guilt. "We have documents, we are going to cite them to you, we are going to show them to you on the ELMO and ask you what you think about it, we will ask a few questions". Whereas, since yesterday, we are trying to ask things through small questions in order to get to small details which are attempting through contradictions, one after the other, attempting to destabilise the witnesses. What will happen two years from now? I am being a bit long right now. In a year or two, once this trial is complete, the judges will have thousands of pages in front of them in which on page 3833 there will be a slight destabilisation of the testimony of Mr. Ahmic. Do you think we can make justice progress that way? I do not believe so. You have your strategy, you have just explained it, it is very important. Present it, ask your questions. The Tribunal will come to the conclusions it needs to. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I will skip the question of the refugees and move on. I will ask a series of names and I will ask Mr. Ahmic to try to remember whether these persons were members of the BH-Army or the village watches. Alaga Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in the BH-Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Asim Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Asim Ahmic, I think he was not in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How about the village watch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was not. He was a cobbler, he stayed at home mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Behbija Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Ejub Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Fadil Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in the BH-Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And his three sons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had two sons -- no, Fadil Ahmic, he was not, he was there but yes, his three sons -- no, his two sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Fahrudin Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Fehim Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Hatif Ahmic, who was Latif's brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was rarely in Ahmici, he was mostly in Zenica. He did not do the watch guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And Latif?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He too, they were both on business in Zenica very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Ahmic Husein?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are two Huseins.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The one from lower Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was not a guard, he was giving --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mirsad Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was an older man, he could not be a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was he in Grabovi doing guard duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was killed in the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Nazif Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not give guard duty. I think he worked up in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Where did he work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Nedzib Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He also pursued his business more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Nezir Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nezir was a driver, so he occasionally gave guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Nurija Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Rasim Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was also a member, but he did not give guard duty because he was in Zume and there was no guard duties there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was he a member of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Rejiba Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was an elderly man, so he was not a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Sakib Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are two of them. They were both elderly and they were not members.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were they giving guard duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Suad Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Suljo Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are two, an older and a younger one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The one from lower Ahmici, the younger one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a policeman in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Vehbija Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You asked me about him already.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Zijad Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And Zahid Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a member too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Juniza Brbic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was an elderly man, he was not a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How about guard duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Brbic Midhat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Hazrudin Bilic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Of the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Hidajet Bilic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was an elderly man, he was not a member, but I think he was giving guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mehrudin Bilic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His son, yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Ramo Bilic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Zijad Bilic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a member too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Muharem Djidic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a member too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Edin Kermo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Elvedin Kermo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a younger -- I do not know, I cannot talk about him. He was a younger man.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Fahrudin Kermo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was an elderly man, he was not in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did he have guard duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was he on guard duty on the 16th in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that he was killed while giving the guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Meho Patkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He died before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Halid Pezer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was killed in the initial conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was he a member of the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I doubt it, because he was young.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Osman Pezer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Zakir Pezer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Hajrudin Pjanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was an elderly man, but I think he was a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Muhamed Pjanic, Hajrudin's son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not have a son by the name of Muhamed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Zec Pjanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That person does not exist in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the 16th when the conflict started, was he in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was killed in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did he have a rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When the two men came to your house, two men from Busovaca, the younger one, did you talk to him that the Muslim army would do something in Nezirovici and Dusina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I said, "what is going on?", and then he said, "what the Muslims did in Nezirovici and Dusina". I did not know what they did there and what happened happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The English translation was not good. What did they exactly tell you, the men from Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just what I said, "what yours did".

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who is"yours"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Meaning the Muslims in Dusina and Nezirovici, and that was it, he did not say anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us go back to when you were hiding in that pipe, what distance was it that you saw the soldiers from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first soldier was up the road towards Pirici, five to six metres away from me, and the ones that were arriving from below, they were about five to six metres away from me too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am going to read you from your statement of 3rd February 1995. I would like you to confirm whether this is correct or not. It is page number 7 for the Prosecution: "He saw the word 'Vitezovi' on the patches. On these patches was written: 'Jedinica Specijalne Namjene Vitezovi'. This means 'The Special Assignment Unit Vitezovi'." Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I probably said that at that time, but for the reasons of security, later on I was not 100 per cent sure even then, so I just limited myself to saying the "Jedinici Specijalne Namjene", so you can check the statement -- can delete it from the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How long did you hear the shooting going on in Ahmici? When did the shooting stop? Can you define that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I did not hear the shooting. I only heard the mortars and the anti-aircraft gun. I did not hear the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Later from conversations with the survivors in Ahmici, did you learn who attacked Ahmici, from which side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think from the east, the units from Busovaca and from the west, the units from Vitez, and I described them already, and from the southern side, the special units and I also described them, the HVO and the HV and they were extremely well equipped. In Grabovi, I cannot tell exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it true that earlier you define that what happened from the Busovaca side was the Jokers were the ones who attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what I heard, so I am just relating what I have heard from others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you were detained together with the civilians were you requested to go to the UNPROFOR base to get two lorries there to transport the civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, while I was in Zume. Three soldiers came and asked who could, among the men, go with them to look for trucks to transfer people to Zenica. I was in favour of that, but as I got up, I felt dizzy, so I could not go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, you said that you noticed some women being raped in the school. Can you tell us on what basis you came to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was talking about that yesterday, I do not know whether you understood me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But my question is: what led you to come to such a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you everything. The man who was lying next to me, his wife was in a separate room and one morning she came in crying, telling him what had happened. I concluded from that what it was about, and after the war, I learnt, and there will probably be witnesses, women who were raped who will come here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You gave us a list of people killed and whose houses you showed us. How did you learn that they had been killed? Did you see that, or did you learn it after the event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the event, when I got to Zenica, this list was made and published of all the people who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So your information comes from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but the house where I was in where they threw a grenade at me, there were two bodies there, two men were lying there dead and burnt. I forgot to mention that. That was in the house where they threw a hand grenade at me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you recognise those bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not, but I learnt afterwards that two men had been killed in that house because they were hidden by the rubble.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let me read you from your statement to the investigators: "In my part of the village" -- this comes at the end of the statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, could Mr. Nobilo at least indicate what page of the statement he is reading from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, would you please give us the page reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I have the Croatian translation, but I shall try and find it in the English text.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have to say it is actually very clear he is reading from a translation because it is completely different from the statement I have in front of me. I have not mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is a translation from the translation department of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I can read the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are speaking at the same time. Are we talking about an exhibit which was given in English from the Prosecution to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I will read it in English, though we have received a translation from the Tribunal as well. I am referring to page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I am not going to make anything of this, Mr. Hayman is losing his temper. The simple point is that what is being read is not exactly the same as the English version, but we will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to ask you a question, the question which you are going to ask, because now I am going to intervene more, you are planning to challenge the deaths that the witness had indicated. Can you tell us what your objective is?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No, I wish to establish who were the HVO commanders in the hamlets and how they treated the civilian victims. That is the crux of my cross-examination and it will bring me to the end of that. Mr. Ahmic, let me try and read this in my bad English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman may substitute Mr. Nobilo for the English language. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: For this limited purpose, your Honour: "In my part of the village, Milicivic Slavko was HVO commander".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please do not read too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will start again: "In my part of the village, Milicivic Slavko was HVO commander. I think he approved the killing of women and children there. In Zume, Papic Zarko, HVO commander, disapproved of killing women and children. In Nadioci, Perkovic Branko, HVO commander, allowed the killing of all civilians. Kupreskic Zoran was HVO commander in Grabovi, and approved of killing of women and children. He was responsible for the killing of my mother and my three sisters, because they happened to be in that area. Santic Nenad was HVO commander of Zume below the road. He was well known as an extremist. He was known as one of the worst ones. It is said that he directly commanded the attack on Ahmici. Kupreskic Vlatko, who most probably led the intelligence of this attack and also most probably took part in it. I know these men from my time in the Territorial Defence before the first conflict."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: My question is: is that true? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was expressing my personal opinion about these people. I have no proof to show that they were commanders, but in my personal conviction they were among the organisers of the Croatian guards, and I know that in Zume women and children were not killed. But the settlement where I lived, near the road, women and children were killed. That is in Grabovi. You know very well when an army comes from an area extraneous to the region had guides and I heard Drago Papic say, "do not kill women and children". I heard that later, but these people probably said, "everyone here has to be killed", so that is my personal view of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just one more question, I will not bother you any more. Line 7, when the soldiers were passing by the road, this is Exhibit 115, did you hide in the ditch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you show me what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So when the soldiers were passing along line 7, where were you when you were watching them? Were you in that pipe, in the water, kneeling, where were you, or lying down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they got close to me, only my head showed, and when they passed, I would get up, so that they would not see my shadow, and they came very close to me. I was about two metres near the end of this pipe, and then they came very close and turned to the other side. So they were about five or six metres away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ahmic. That ends my cross-examination. Thank you, Mr. President, for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have a few questions, your Honour. Now might be an appropriate time if you wish to take a break. It is now 11.13, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. I was so involved in this discussion that I did not note the time. All right, we will resume at 11.30. (11.15 am) (A short break) (11.30 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I only have a few questions for the witness. Good morning, Mr. Ahmic. Thank you so much for your patience and calmness in answering all these questions. I just have a few matters to clear up with you. The Defence in their cross-examination of you referred at some length to the Territorial Defence in the village of Ahmici. Was service in the Territorial Defence voluntary or compulsory in the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Service in the Territorial Defence was not compulsory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: For those who were serving in the Territorial Defence, was there any disciplinary process if they failed to attend for duty on any particular day, if they failed to attend their watch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So if a member of the watch slept in one morning, then nothing was done about the fact that that man did not attend for duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, absolutely nothing. It was more on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think after you fled from Ahmici you served in the Bosnian army, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was expelled from Ahmici. Yes, I was in the BH-Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I am sorry, you are quite correct. You were expelled from Ahmici. Can you compare the Bosnian army in which you served after you were expelled from Ahmici with the Territorial Defence which existed in your village?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are objecting because this opens a new question of the quality of the BH-Army after 16th April 1993, so it is a completely new area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The Defence, Mr. President, in their cross-examination, are trying to establish that there was an organised, well equipped military unit in the village of Ahmici. The Prosecutor's position is that this was simply not the case. We have here in front of us a man who served in the Bosnian army in 1995 and 1996. I think he is in a position, very briefly, to compare the Bosnian army in which he served in 1995 and 1996 with the village guard which he was in in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I rather tend to believe that Mr. Nobilo is correct. We are not going to redo the examination, Mr. Ahmic has now been examined, cross-examined and re-examined since 12.10 yesterday. If questions about the comparison between the HVO and Bosnian army have still not been made clear, then the judges will not understand it either. I think we do understand. Please go on. In any case, excuse me for slowing things down myself here, this goes back to the question of this morning. A time will come when the judges will decide, they themselves, which questions are being asked properly. It is true these comparisons might be important, but this was already raised. We are not going to use the re-examination to restart the examination-in-chief. Please move to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did the Territorial Defence in the village of Ahmici receive supplies and ammunition from the town of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but very, very little came.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many members of the village watch wore uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were only about a dozen people who had uniforms, but they made them themselves from tent material, but we hardly had any original military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Would you describe the Territorial Defence in Ahmici as disorganised or organised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was more a disorganised army than an organised army that I was in in 1993, 1994 and 1995. There is a big difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When the Bosnian army was established at the end of 1992, did this disorganisation continue in the village of Ahmici within the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already spoken about that. The organisation was similar to the organisation of the Territorial Defence, because there was no regular supplies of military material and ammunition. These battalions, companies and things were formed on paper, so I would rather not go into those questions any more. There was not sufficient military material, one could have had anything on paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The witness has already answered that. You are going back to the question which he has just delineated five minutes ago. Please, move to another type of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will move on. It is a re-examination, the Prosecutor does have the right to cover ground that was asked in examination-in-chief. I am not going to press my rights before the court and I say that very respectfully before you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I do not think, Mr. Cayley, that we are going to get into a question and a trial where the Prosecutor is going to ask the same questions again. We will not get anywhere. I think the judges are here in order to make sure how the time is being used and to get to what is the absolute essential thing, which is the accusations against General Blaskic. You have the right to ask questions, but in relation to what Mr. Nobilo has asked during his cross-examination. Continue, please, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, when your father and brother were murdered outside your house, do you believe that the soldiers who did that act were acting according to orders, or do you believe that they simply decided of their own will to kill your father and your brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my statement, in all my statements, they did it exclusively according to military orders, because that is what they said, "do as you are ordered". He refused and then he said, "take care, I will carry out the orders", and then he did what he did, so this was clearly a strict military order received from somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions of the witness. I now offer the witness to the judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. Thank you for having attempted to understand what the judges were trying to say through me. I now turn to my colleagues, Judge Riad, I am sure you have some questions. Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Abdulah Ahmic. I would like you, as much as you can, to give me some clear answers to a few questions which I would like to ask you. I gathered from your testimony, and from the pictures we had, that all Muslim houses which you showed us were being burnt, and that it was systematic. Was there any criterion in the choice of these houses, or was it just a total coverage of all the Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were a couple of houses that were not set on fire, but a very small number that one can count on the fingers of one hand, but I think there were hundreds of houses that were set on fire and destroyed. I do not know whether there was any particular reason why they did not set fire to those five houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Five houses. So it was a very small exception?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were very few Muslim houses that were not destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were the people in the houses when it was burnt up or were they killed fighting? Was there any fight to defend themselves or was there any reason for the burning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think judging by what happened in my case in the settlement of Zume, I think the identical thing occurred elsewhere. There was some resistance around the mosque, there were some people putting up some minor resistance, and luckily UNPROFOR came and protected those men, otherwise they would have run out of ammunition and they would have all been killed. There were many women and children there. In the village of Grabovi, there was a classical attack, there was no resistance there either.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The people inside, the men were not armed, were not attacking anybody, in the majority of the houses? Were they burnt inside the houses or were the houses burnt without people inside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that most of the people were taken out of their houses and killed and in my opinion, when they set fire to the houses, they put them back inside to cover up their traces, because mostly the corpses could not be identified, so they killed them in front of their houses, then they took them back inside to burn, because there were quite a number of corpses that were unidentified and that were buried. I think that is how they proceeded. I too would have probably been put back into my house to burn and then you could just find a couple of burnt bones at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In conclusion to what you said, there was some kind of similarity of method, it was the same method applied to all the houses and not sporadic and individual attacks which were different from one to another?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a simultaneous attack, at the same time they attacked, or rather very little difference. First it started in Grabovi, then the lower part of the village. When they attacked the central part of the village, they blocked the way so there was no way for us to escape northwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You lost all your family, as you said. You mentioned -- you had a big family, the Ahmic family apparently, Sukrija, Sakib, Fahrudin, your father and then you had Muris, you had your little sister too, I think, you lost everybody big and small.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lost three sisters, they were young girls. They were girls.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the others were cousins, uncles? Apparently the family lived all over Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was your family a prominent family in Ahmici? Did it have any role socially speaking, politically speaking, or were these people chosen specially to be persecuted, or was it just among the whole persecution of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as my family is concerned, out of us six children, we were all very good pupils. My brother graduated from the university in Tuzla with greatest honours. He was the best student they had, so that ours was a progressive family. The whole population was well educated and had their own culture and they were all killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But there was no special reason to address this kind of persecution to your family in particular? It was part of a general policy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was also due to my brother Muris's participation in the Territorial Defence, where he was a commander, so somebody who saw my mother and sisters decided to kill them because of Muris, because he was one of the organisers. That may have been a reason, but the fact is that other women and children were killed, so one cannot say that my family was specially targeted. All the families were targeted. In some cases, they did not kill the women and children, in others they did, but the men were all targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You just mentioned a few minutes ago, you said that some commanders approved of the killing of women and children and some other commanders did not approve of the killing of women and children. Did they all approve of the killing of unarmed civilians? Was it a general policy to kill unarmed civilians, at least men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is very easy to establish that the men who were killed in Zume that I have listed, they were formally in the BH-Army. They were all people like my brother Muris in civilian clothing, unarmed. They were in the formal sense members of the army, but they were killed as civilians. If they had been soldiers, they would have resisted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: They were not killed fighting, they were killed unarmed and not fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were unarmed, they were not allowed to have arms in the part where we lived. One may have had arms secretly, but few people had weapons, because if we had had them, we would have put up resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You yourself, when you were shot in the head, was it a result of a fight or were you unarmed and it was some kind of execution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken out like a dog and I was shot at from a distance of one metre. That is how they behaved.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Then at a certain moment, I cannot exactly give the details, you were lying down and there was a tall man and a short man and the tall man asked the other one to kill you, was that right, to shoot you and told him --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- "you have to follow orders", that was your words, "you have to follow orders". Did you understand whose orders it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not the orders of the tall man to the shorter one, but they were referring to the orders of their commander, because later on he said, "I will carry out the orders and you will have to account for this". He threatened him, so it was a military order that they were carrying out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was it an order to, if you understood rightly, to kill you in particular or to kill all men, all Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was killed in that way, my father, so I do not have the exact report as to how my brother was killed, probably similarly he was taken out of the basement and shot. I think that all the men were killed like that. A house would be surrounded, they would surround the house, order people to come out and just shoot them, because we were in a situation that we had no way out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I believe in the beginning of your testimony you mentioned that you were living in peace with the Croats and that everything started in April, the whole thing started 16th April or around that period. At the same time, you mentioned that the HVO was a power involved in all walks of life. Did you notice that the HVO was making some propaganda against the Muslims, was preparing the Croats psychologically to attack the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they set up their television and radio in Vitez and they systematically prepared their people for the attack on the Muslims. Because in Central Bosnia, they were not waging war against the Serbs, they took out the army to Kuber, a peak in Mescema above Travnik. The Muslims held the lines towards the Serbs and they were behind the Muslims. They were laying mines in the event the Chetniks, the Serbs would attack. Then the Muslims would come across their mines and they held the lines behind the Muslims. I do not know why they were at Kuber, there were very strong formations there and that was 200 metres from the frontline with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: 200 metres or kilometres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 200 kilometres, I apologise, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad. Judge Shahabuddeen will now also ask you a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, you remember the part of your testimony to which you have indeed referred more than once, concerning your hiding in a hollow or in a pipe near the point number 4 by the road side; you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you were there, you saw two groups of soldiers dressed in different uniforms, I think. Could each of those two groups see the other group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw three groups, the first group that was coming from the upper end of the road towards the village of Pirici and they land up close to me; then another group in original Ustasha uniforms from the Second World War that they used. Of course, they must have made them later. Those are the two groups, and then from the lower end of the road there were five or six groups consisting of about ten well armed soldiers and they came consecutively.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Several groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could each group see the other groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The group coming from the lower end of the road could not see those from the upper end, only if they climbed up on to the road they could see each other. Yes, they could see each other, because they were passing, they climbed up on a slope and then they could see each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: My impression from what you said is that the groups were not fighting each other, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the Croatian groups amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You described several groups, I am asking you whether each of those groups was fighting with the other groups. Was there any kind of military confrontation amongst those various groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. One could have heard that. If there was any fire exchanged by them, I would have heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was it your impression that those different groups were co-operating with each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They could have linked up together, there was only ten metres distance between them, so they could approach one another. The only thing is that they did not go under the bridge, they probably joined up above me on top.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: At various stages in your evidence, you refer to different groups. Was it your impression that those groups, by that I mean military groups, were pursuing a common programme, common aims and common objectives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most probably their aim was to stifle all resistance. These were coming from the south, these others from the west, and their objective was to capture the area around the mosque, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question about -- do forgive me if I do not have the names correctly, but I am referring to two people by the names which I have given them in my notebook of Ivo Papic and Simo Vidovic, two people to whom you called out at one point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Papic Ivo and Simo Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You asked them to save you and they said, "come with us", do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Those two people were Croats, or were they Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were Croats, elderly men.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In your experience of the situation, did you see or hear of other incidents in which other Croats reached out to help Muslims who were in distress?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were such cases, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Answer me please one last question. The BH-Army was the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the legal formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The legal formation. Now was that army in existence before the formation of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO was the first to be formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The HVO was formed before the BH-Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, quite a bit before, maybe one or two years before the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The BH-Army was formed one or two years before the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I see. Now the HVO army was formed before the BH-Army, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness nodded).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have a clarification I would like to ask. You alluded to changes in the curriculum in the schools. I did not quite understand that, because you spoke about a period which seems rather short to me, short for changing curriculum. Was this something that was done in schools, or were there instructions that came that the curriculum was supposed to be changed. How did things take place in actual fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was easy for Croats to change the curriculum, because the text books were coming from the Republic of Croatia, and they continued working on the basis of those programmes. They probably had some difficulty in adjusting it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I suppose it was the contents of the history courses that were changed, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly the language, history, and these social sciences, the arts. Of course the natural sciences were more or less similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: At some point, you said that between August 1992 and April 1993, a great deal of military material was collected, specifically in different homes. What is your perception of that? Did you suspect something was happening, did people talk about this, among friends, "did you see it, was it at night", because this was a very significant amount of material, according to what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can tell you that I saw with my own eyes ammunition being unloaded. My neighbour, Zoran Papic, had quite a large warehouse near his house, he had a car and he often brought it in. Then once I saw a large military truck from Busovaca, and ammunition was being unloaded to the house of the Kupreskics, Ivica Kupreskic's house, there in the cellar there was a large quantity of ammunition being unloaded. I could not be close by, but one could see. Military ammunition is usually packed in green crates, in green boxes so one could see even from a distance that this was military equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ahmic. This long testimony before the Tribunal is now complete and we are very sensitive to the fact that you came, especially in light of the suffering which you experienced, you and your entire family. The Tribunal will now allow you to return to your home and hopes that if possible, you will find some peace and calm. Registrar, could we have Mr. Ahmic taken out of the room so that he may leave. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I think it is Mr. Harmon who is getting up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President and good morning, your Honours. Our next witness will be Witness G, a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: G you said, is that right? Yes, G. Before the witness comes in, I suppose that the curtains should be drawn.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to say for the public who is watching that the following witness will be called Witness G We will lower the curtains, which will allow the witness to come in from that side, and once seated, the person can be hidden, after which the curtains will be raised again. (Pause). (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated, Witness G You are going to read the declaration, which will be given to you. Please go ahead. You may remain seated. Witness G, please read the declaration. WITNESS G (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness G, as part of this trial before the Tribunal, against Colonel Blaskic who is here, you have been called to testify. You may speak without hatred, without fear, without any concern. You are under the protection of the Tribunal, special protective measures have been provided for you here and outside the walls of the Tribunal. Mr. Prosecutor? To ensure your complete identification, the Registrar will show your identity on a piece of paper and this way the Tribunal will be sure that in fact you are the correct person. Is that all right? Fine. Since the Tribunal does not know your name, it is better that way. Unfortunately, we will refer to you as Witness G, but this is for your safety. Please try to relax and you will first answer questions asked by the Prosecutor. You know that this is a Tribunal and then the Defence attorneys will ask you questions as well. It is now 12.15. Mr. Harmon, about how much time have you planned for your examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Not more than two hours, your Honour. Probably less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. The Tribunal asks that you get to the essentials so that the amount of time spent by the Tribunal here is not overly long. Proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness G

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you some background questions first. Are you a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How old are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Ahmici, in the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In the Zume section of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Have you lived in Ahmici all your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the judges about your educational background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I completed the elementary school and then the secondary school for machinery and then I studied in Zenica for two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have the assistance of the usher, Mr. President, in placing Prosecutor's Exhibit 119A on the ELMO and distributing to counsel. Mr. President and counsel, 119A is an enlargement of a portion of Exhibit 50, with various locations marked on it, and 119B is a legend associated with the numbers that are found on 119A. Mr. Usher, if that could be moved to the left? That is fine, thank you, for right now. Let me ask you first of all -- have you had an opportunity to indicate to me certain locations that will be relevant to your testimony this morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to see Prosecutor's Exhibit 119A before coming into court, and are the locations that you indicated to me marked on this particular exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In respect of Prosecutor's Exhibit 119B, which you do not have before you, but which is a legend, did you assist me in the preparation of that legend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now if I could, Witness G, if I could ask you first of all to focus your attention on 15th April 1993, the day before the attack. Where were you living? Can you point the court on the Exhibit 119A to the location of your house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
